clue.text: Capital mostly left yacht for sailing — it gives a human feel to things

definitions.text: it gives a human feel to things

indicators.note: most of something is not all of it, so the final letter of the word is dropped
letters that go sailing are tossed about on the waves and end up rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the word taken as written, minus its final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor with money to spare leaves most of it behind to take a yacht out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital mostly' tempts you to shorten the capital, but 'mostly' clips only 'left'; CAPITAL goes into the mix whole with YACHT.
explanation.definitionFit: The pathetic fallacy is the literary device of attributing human emotions to nature or objects, such as an angry sea or weeping skies.

clue.text: Shoe with too much tripping up after steps

parts.note: a stile is a set of steps for climbing over a fence

indicators.note: in a down clue, something going up reads from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: OTT is short for over the top, meaning excessive

explanation.surface: Someone in shoes with too much heel stumbles after coming down some steps.
explanation.walkthrough: A stile is the step or ladder over a field fence, common on British footpaths; 'after steps' places the reversed piece behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiletto is a woman's shoe with a very high, thin heel, named after the slender dagger.

clue.text: Start to supply bogus protective garment

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
mock means imitation or fake

explanation.surface: A fraudster begins supplying fake protective clothing, a nod to the puzzle's PPE scandal theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start to supply' reads like beginning a delivery, but it just supplies the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A smock is a loose overall worn over clothes to keep them clean, as by painters or farm workers.

clue.text: Set up firm ignoring hospital guideline

parts.note: to stand something is to set it upright

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: firm and hard both mean solid
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A company is founded that pays no attention to hospital guidance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up firm' looks like founding a business; it is two separate pieces, a verb and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a rule or level that work is expected to meet, so it serves as a guideline.

clue.text: Nicks a lot

definitions.meaning: first meaning: makes small cuts or notches in

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone who steals often, since nick is British slang for steal; here nicks are small cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: To score a surface is to mark it with lines or cuts, and scores of things means very many of them.

clue.text: Borrow and steal — one might hold file for woman?

definitions.text: one might hold file for woman?

parts.note: to sponge is to borrow or scrounge without paying back
to bag something is to grab or take it

explanation.surface: Borrowing and stealing a file suggests a spy lifting documents for a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The file is not a dossier but a nail file; a sponge bag is British for a toiletries bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A toiletries bag holds grooming items such as a nail file, hence the question mark on this playful description.

clue.text: Attractive one, entrepreneur getting caught

indicators.note: to catch a remark is to hear it, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a magnate is a wealthy, powerful business person

explanation.surface: A charming business figure ends up caught out, fitting the puzzle's scandal theme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting caught' sounds like an arrest, but it means being heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet pulls iron towards itself, literally exerting attraction, so it is an attractive object.

clue.text: Seeing defect in old scrubs online getting flogged

indicators.note: something flogged is beaten about, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone spots a flaw in secondhand medical scrubs being sold on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: Flogged is British slang for sold, which fits 'online'; its other sense, beaten, is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Colour blindness is an inherited vision condition in which a person cannot tell certain hues apart.

clue.text: A suit without protection? Michelle Mone attracts free money from these

indicators.note: letters set free are loosed from their order and can fall into a new one

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the outside letters act as a protective casing, so stripping them leaves only the inside

parts.note: the word's inside letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawsuit over PPE profits accuses Michelle Mone of attracting free money.
explanation.walkthrough: Baroness Michelle Mone is a British businesswoman whose firm faced a suit over a government PPE contract; her name is simply letters for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash machines dispense banknotes to customers, so these are where people withdraw money, the full formal name for ATMs.

clue.text: Soft spot essentially around Scotsman

indicators.note: going around something means enclosing it, so one piece wraps the other
the essence of a word is its core, so only the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the word's central letters
Ian is the crossword's stock Scottish first name

explanation.surface: Someone admits to having a real fondness for a Scottish man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft spot' reads as one phrase, a liking; split it, and 'Soft' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In musical notation piano is the Italian direction to play quietly, so it means soft.

clue.text: That man left one to swindle for large bit of brass

parts.note: the pronoun for a man
L is the abbreviation for left
I is the Roman numeral one
to con someone is to swindle them

explanation.surface: A man abandons someone to cheat them out of a big pile of money.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass is British slang for money, which the surface uses; the definition means a brass instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A helicon is a large tuba-like instrument coiled around the player's body, a big member of the brass section.

clue.text: Career? Enthusiastic about encounter

parts.note: to career is to rush along headlong
to be into something is to be keen on it

explanation.surface: Someone is asked whether they are passionate about their job and meeting people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' looks like a noun meaning a profession; it is the verb meaning to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: To run into someone is to meet them by chance, an idiom meaning to come across or meet.

clue.text: Joins numbers of illegal sellers without uniform

indicators.note: to be without something is to lack it, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: touts sell tickets unofficially at inflated prices
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Plainclothes figures link up with gangs of illicit street vendors.
explanation.walkthrough: A tout, in Britain, is someone reselling tickets outside a venue; 'Joins numbers' is a slightly cryptic way of saying adds up.
explanation.definitionFit: To tot up is to add figures together, so tots means combines numbers into a total.

clue.text: Test protection — it might maximise profits

parts.note: to tax something is to strain or test it
shelter is cover or protection

explanation.surface: A trial of a protective product promises big returns.
explanation.walkthrough: Tax here is the verb meaning to make demands on, as in taxing your patience.
explanation.definitionFit: A tax shelter is an arrangement that legally reduces tax owed, so more of the earnings are kept.

clue.text: As big character in court through trial

parts.note: someone up before the judge is in court
per means by way of or through
a court case is a trial

explanation.surface: A larger-than-life personality appears before the court throughout a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big character' sounds like a colourful person, but it is a capital letter; 'in court' is up, as in up before the magistrate.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper-case letters are capitals, the large forms of the alphabet, so text set that way appears as big letters.

clue.text: Severed company to protect husband: PPE director

indicators.note: a guard protects by surrounding, so one piece is placed around another

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company
H is the abbreviation for husband
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for director

explanation.surface: A company cuts ties to shield a spouse who ran a PPE firm, echoing the Mone scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: PPE, personal protective equipment, is lifted straight from the clue as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something chopped has been cut through with a blow, so it is cut off or separated.

clue.text: Mone reportedly loaded, not quite expressing sorrow

indicators.note: falling just short of complete means the final letter is lost
what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: the surname is pronounced like the word for a groan
loaded means filled up

explanation.surface: Michelle Mone, said to be rich, is not quite sorry about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' plays on its slang sense of wealthy; for the wordplay it means full.
explanation.definitionFit: Moanful means mournful or plaintive, the adjective for someone whose voice is full of lament and grief.

clue.text: See 9 Across
Deal with member over request for item of PPE

parts.note: to face a problem is to confront it
M is the abbreviation for member
an ask is a request

explanation.surface: An MP handles a request for protective equipment, echoing the pandemic contracts scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the member on top of the request.
explanation.definitionFit: A mask worn over the nose and mouth is standard personal protective equipment in hospitals.

clue.text: Certain PPE is fake — one should be serving time?

indicators.note: something fake is made up, so these letters are made up into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Some protective equipment turns out to be counterfeit, so whoever supplied it belongs in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serving time' suggests a jail sentence; it is serving an apprenticeship, the fixed training term.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice learns a trade under a master for a set period, historically bound by indenture.

clue.text: Greedy person: slippery one getting bird

parts.note: a pig is a glutton

indicators.note: something slippery slides about and will not hold its shape, so the letters shift

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A greedy, slippery character gets a reward, a jab at the puzzle's profiteers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greedy person' looks like the definition in a scandal-themed puzzle; it is wordplay, and 'bird' at the end defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The pigeon is a common grey bird of towns and cities, a member of the dove family.

clue.text: See 9 Across
Famous person is one Tory

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
Con is short for Conservative, the Tory party

explanation.surface: A celebrity turns out to be a Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party; Mone sat as a Conservative peer.
explanation.definitionFit: An icon is a celebrated figure widely admired as a symbol of something, so a very well-known person.

clue.text: Business woman taking last of Tory cash

parts.note: Michelle Mone, the businesswoman in this puzzle's theme

indicators.note: the last of something is its final part, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the word's closing letter

explanation.surface: A female entrepreneur pockets Conservative party funds.
explanation.walkthrough: The business woman is the theme's Michelle Mone, a lingerie entrepreneur turned Conservative peer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash is money in the form of notes and coins, so the two words are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Bar to restrict fighting suit? That's reasonable

indicators.note: restricting something means hemming it in, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a local is one's neighbourhood pub
a gi is the jacket and trousers worn for judo or karate

explanation.surface: A ban on lawsuits over a fight is proposed as a sensible measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' and 'suit' pose as a legal ban and a lawsuit; in Britain the local is your regular pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Logical describes thinking that follows sound reasoning, so it means sensible or rational.

clue.text: Press husband? It's a tough challenge

parts.note: to iron clothes is to press them
one's man is one's husband

explanation.surface: Pushing your husband into doing the ironing is tough going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press husband' suggests nagging a spouse; it is two separate words, a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ironman is a gruelling endurance triathlon of long swim, cycle and marathon run.

clue.text: Blocks opening of Covid records

indicators.note: an opening is where a thing begins, so its first letter is taken

parts.note: the word's first letter
logs are written records

explanation.surface: Someone prevents the release of pandemic-era documents, a nod to Covid inquiry disputes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blocks' reads as a verb for obstructing access; it keeps that sense but defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To clog a pipe or passage is to obstruct it, so clogs means obstructs or jams.

clue.text: Break even in different business at last

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside, enclosed

parts.note: else means other or different
taken as written

indicators.note: at the last means at the very end, so only the closing letter counts

parts.note: the word's final letter

explanation.surface: A firm that has changed direction finally manages to break even.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break even' is a single phrase in the surface; split it, and 'Break' alone is the definition. Elevenses is a British mid-morning snack break.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a short pause for tea and biscuits around eleven in the morning, so it is a rest break.
